messages.body_plain:
Dear Roy, 

> Firstly, for a normal PCA (dudi.pca), is it possible to see the contribution of alleles/loci to the first PC?

$c1; please see the doc (vignette("adegenet-basics"), p.42-43).

> Secondly, in sPCA, what is the difference between the actual scores (myspca$li) and lagged scores (myspca$ls)?

Let 'x' be the vector of a given principal component (or any real-valued vector in) and W be a matrix of spatial weights. The line "i" of W contains spatial weights defining proximities of all locations to location "i". Then, the lag vector 'y' is simply given by 'y=Wx'.

That is, any value at a given location is replaced by the average value computed on neighbouring locations. Maps of lagged variables are thus smoothed, sometimes allowing to clarify spatial structures.

Cheers

Thibaut.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Avik, 

In the case you describe (two demes + hybrids), you would more probably expect K=2, not K=3.

The error in your code is that x1 and x2 are not genind objects, butvectors of integers returned by "which". A correct code would be:
###
x1 <- dat[grp==1]
x2 <- dat[grp==2]
###

where dat is your original genind object; alternatively, if grp has just groups 1 and 2:
temp <- seppop(dat, grp)
###
x1 <- temp[[1]]
x2<- temp[[2]]
###

About your last question: DAPC always has K-1 discriminant functions at most, K being the number of clusters. Therefore, for K=2, you'll end up with only on discriminant function, and no scatterplot as you'd need two axes to get one. Note that 'scatter' adapts automatically and uses a more appropriate representation when there is just one axis to be plotted.

Cheers

Thibaut.

In the case you describe (two demes + hybrids), you would more probably expect K=2, not K=3.

x2 <- dat[grp==2]

temp <- seppop(dat, grp)
###

x2<- temp[[2]]
###

About your last question: DAPC always has K-1 discriminant functions at most, K being the number of clusters. Hello, 

yes, the problem is that you left the first column reading 913,914, etc. meaning as many copies of second allele. There is no limitation as to the ploidy of the data in genlight objects, and this is a pretty good illustration.

You need to provide the constructor (new) with a matrix of nb of alleles ONLY as first argument; for instance:
###
x<- new("genlight", SNPmerge[,-(1:3)], indNames = SNPmerge$sampleName, pop = SNPmerge$PopID, ploidy=2)
###

Hope this helps.

Cheers

Thibaut.
